synthesis.positioning_statement:
Generic early-warning signals (EWS) of critical slowing down, rising lag-1 autocorrelation and variance, have been tested on ecological monitoring data for more than a decade, and the largest tests have been sobering. Burthe et al. (2016) tallied true positives, false negatives and false positives for variance and autocorrelation across 126 abundance series from six UK aquatic systems within a 10-year association window and found false positives more prevalent than false negatives and true positives in fewer than one series in ten. O'Brien et al. (2023) evaluated classical, multivariate and machine-learning (EWSNet; Deb et al. 2022) indicators in transitioning and non-transitioning lake plankton series and reported that most indicators performed no better than a 0.5 chance reference, with unscaled EWSNet reaching true-positive probabilities of about 0.9 only at true-negative probabilities of 0.05-0.19. In fisheries, Zhang (2020) evaluated standard deviation and AR1 against productivity regime shifts in 191 RAM Legacy populations with an explicit true-negative and positive-likelihood-ratio framing; Cano, Jensen and Dakos (2025) trained boosted regression trees on a "dynamical footprint" that includes AR1 and SD across RAM Legacy, ICES cod and FishGlob series and obtained leave-one-out AUCs of 0.84, 0.75 and 0.65; and Pélissié et al. (2026) showed that abrupt productivity declines in 315 assessed stocks were followed by biomass collapse in 11 of 42 cases (26%), negative shifts being present in 23% of collapsed and 12% of non-collapsed stocks. Whole-lake experiments (Pace et al. 2017; Wilkinson et al. 2018; Buelo et al. 2022) and laboratory systems (Drake and Griffen 2010; Jarvis-Cross et al. 2025; Cerini et al. 2025) supply reference systems or controls and explicit true- versus false-alarm rates. We therefore do not claim that prior work ignored false positives or non-transitioning series, nor that AR1/variance-type indicators have not been applied to RAM Legacy or FishGlob at scale; each of those has been done.

What has not been done, to our knowledge, is to ask whether a prespecified EWS score adds detection of first population-abundance collapses beyond what the current state and recent trend of the same series already provide, at a common false-alarm burden, in a design that is time-indexed and complete in follow-up. Every empirical EWS evaluation above is retrospective or static. Burthe et al. and O'Brien et al. classify whole series after the fact; Zhang locates shifts in the full record and looks back; Cano et al. assign one footprint and one class per series, validate across series rather than across time, and relabel non-abrupt series predicted abrupt as 50 populations "at risk" with no follow-up window; Pélissié et al. date shifts with hindsight and report a relative risk rather than a calibrated alarm. None scores a state-or-trend comparator on the same origins. The forecasting literature supplies that comparator but has not connected it to EWS: Ward et al. (2014) showed on 2379 vertebrate series that a random walk without drift is essentially unbeatable at 1-5-year horizons; Holmes et al. (2007) validated diffusion-approximation quasi-extinction forecasts from 20-year parameterization windows; Hefley et al. (2013) paired an indicator with a state-space threshold-crossing model in a single quail population; and Pinsky and Byler (2015) predicted collapse across 154 RAM Legacy populations from fishing pressure, growth rate and climate variability without any EWS. Machine-learning EWS work has the evaluation machinery we borrow. Bury et al. (2021) and Ma et al. (2025) report ROC or sensitivity and specificity against variance and AR1; Falmagne et al. (2026) detect half of transitions within a fixed window at a 3.6% false-positive rate on a held-out year; Deb et al. (2022) compare EWSNet with logistic regression, SVM, random forest and MLP. But its negatives are surrogates, nulls or non-ecological systems, every comparator is itself fed EWS features, and no study uses monitored population series with a calendar horizon. Outside ecology, Mullett (2026) evaluates detectors under a locked equal-false-positive contract, and the seizure-prediction and landmarking literatures define sensitivity at a fixed false-prediction rate with event-time surrogates; we import these conventions rather than reinvent them.

Our contribution is therefore the combination, not any single element: (i) sequential forecast origins at which every predictor uses only data available by that year; (ii) fixed 1-5-year horizons with negatives requiring complete follow-up, so that right-censored origins are never counted as non-events, a treatment not visible in any anchor paper; (iii) alarm thresholds for the EWS score and for a capacity-matched state-and-trend baseline (abundance relative to reference, recent slope, a local-linear state-space threshold-crossing forecast, and a last-value score after Ward et al.) calibrated in development data to the same false-alarm budget; and (iv) evaluation grouped by biological system across RAM Legacy, survey indices, GPDD, the Living Planet Database and BioTIME, with lake regime shifts as a separate challenge analysis positioned against O'Brien et al. (2023). The quantities Cano et al. and Pélissié et al. report, 50 at-risk populations without later verification and a 26% positive predictive fraction with no comparator, are exactly what an operating-point analysis against a matched baseline is designed to adjudicate, and Boettiger and Hastings' (2012) warning against selecting systems because they transitioned is answered by the risk-set design.

Two caveats bound the claim. First, every judgment about prior designs rests on abstracts, search snippets and public code; full text was read only for Ward et al. (2014) and Lapeyrolerie and Boettiger (2023). The methods of Zhang (2020), Cano et al. (2025) and Pélissié et al. (2026), especially pre-shift windowing, the operationalization of "no shift" and series-end handling, must be confirmed against the published supplements before the novelty statement is frozen. Second, the search could not reach EcoEvoRxiv, ESA/ICES/ASLO abstracts or the reference list of the 2026 Entropy review, and a very recent sequential-prediction sequel from the Montpellier group cannot be excluded; the claim is made "to our knowledge" and will be re-checked at submission.
synthesis.novelty_reasoning: All four independent lines of evidence in the inputs agree: thirteen topic sweeps (569 raw records, ~485 unique citations), eight anchor-paper design extractions, two adversarial refutations (angles A and B, both equivalent_study_found=false) and the Angle D adjudication (22 merged candidates, none rated equivalent or substantial-overlap) found no 2010-2026 study that combines (i) sequential time-indexed forecast origins with predictors restricted to data available at each origin, (ii) fixed 1-5-year horizons, (iii) temporally out-of-sample evaluation, (iv) a capacity-matched state-and-trend or state-space threshold-crossing baseline scored on the same origins, (v) alarm thresholds calibrated to a common false-alarm budget, and (vi) complete outcome follow-up for negatives, for population-abundance collapse across realms. The closest work each supplies only a subset: Cano et al. 2025 (EWS-type features, RAM/FishGlob, out-of-sample across series, negatives present, but static per-series shape classification, no time hold-out, no baseline, false alarms relabelled 'at risk', no follow-up; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122; code https://github.com/alejvcano/dynfoot2025; confidence high on these design facts because the key-paper extraction read the archived R functions); Pélissié et al. 2026 (same data source and a biomass-defined collapse outcome, explicit 26% positive predictive fraction, but a hindsight change-point predictor and a retrospective relative risk with no baseline or calibration; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/; high); Zhang 2020 (same indicators and database, TP/TN/likelihood-ratio framing, but productivity shifts, no origins, no baseline visible; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1470160X20303083; medium because only the abstract was visible); Burthe 2016 and O'Brien 2023 (explicit false-positive accounting but retrospective per-series classification, no horizon, no baseline; https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43744-8; high); Falmagne 2026 (fixed window, held-out year, explicit 3.6% FPR, but an online game, no state/trend baseline; https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2503493122; high on design, low on author initials); Deb 2022 (learner comparison, but all comparators fed EWS features; https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.211475; medium); Pinsky & Byler 2015 (collapse prediction on RAM Legacy with non-collapsing populations, but no EWS and no visible hold-out; https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/282/1813/20151053/84303/Fishing-fast-growth-and-climate-variability; high); Ward 2014 (random-walk baseline at 1-5 years on 2379 series, single origin, no events; full text read; high). The verdict is 'novel-combination-supported' rather than 'partially-preempted' because no candidate contains the baseline-relative, false-alarm-matched, complete-follow-up element, which is the substantive question; it is not stronger than that because (a) the margin is narrow on data and indicators (Zhang, Cano), (b) all anchor-paper judgments rest on snippets and code, not full text, (c) the third refutation angle (Angle D) ended with its final broad sweep unexecuted and the present synthesis could run zero verification queries (budget 200/200 exhausted), and (d) EcoEvoRxiv and society abstract databases are poorly indexed, so an unindexed sequel cannot be excluded. Hard rule 1 respected: no EWS-outcome association was computed or speculated about for any dataset.

closest_prior_work.citation: Cano, A. V., Jensen, O. P. & Dakos, V. (2025). Identifying fish populations prone to abrupt shifts via dynamical footprint analysis. PNAS 122(34): e2505461122. doi:10.1073/pnas.2505461122. URL https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122 ; code https://github.com/alejvcano/dynfoot2025 (raw zip read by the key-paper extraction). Confidence: high on design facts.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Two of our candidate datasets (RAM Legacy productivity, FishGlob CPUE) plus ICES cod; 9,006 series screened, 629 retained (>=20 y, no gaps); footprint of seven stability metrics including lag-1 AR, SD and CV as whole-series values and Kendall-tau rolling trends (window 50% of series); xgbTree BRT per dataset; leave-one-out CV across series; AUC 0.84/0.75/0.65; non-abrupt series are the negative class with class-wise sensitivity (40% abrupt-class sensitivity in FishGlob).
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Static one-prediction-per-series shape classification (AICc abrupt vs nonabrupt, asdetect-confirmed) rather than first abundance collapse; LOO across series, not across time; footprint trend uses the whole series and code default truncates abrupt-class series at the retrospectively estimated breakpoint (label-informed); no state/trend or null comparator; class = argmax probability with no calibration; nonabrupt series predicted abrupt relabelled 'potential abrupt' (50 populations across 11 LMEs) instead of counted as false alarms, no follow-up window; single realm.

closest_prior_work.citation: Pélissié, M., Devictor, V., Jensen, O. P. & Dakos, V. (2026). Abrupt declines in fish productivity often precede stock collapses in marine fisheries. Science Advances 12(36): eaed7911, published 2 Sep 2026. doi:10.1126/sciadv.aed7911. URLs https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed7911 ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/ ; preprint https://ecoevorxiv.org/repository/view/9253/ ; GitHub https://github.com/matpelissie/ocean_warming_fisheries (existence confirmed via API by refutation B); Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.20059643 (single snippet, medium). Confidence: high on main facts.
closest_prior_work.overlap: 315 RAM Legacy stocks 1950-2020 (median 41 y); collapse defined as biomass below 25% of the to-date average with 10%-of-max, 15% and 50%-of-average sensitivities; productivity abrupt shifts (PAS) in 25.7% of stocks (42 negative, 39 positive); negative PAS in 23% of collapsed vs 12% of non-collapsed stocks; only 11 of 42 negative-PAS stocks (26%) later collapsed; most negative PAS 4-12 y before collapse (abstract: about a decade; press: on average 12 y; preprint: 10-20 y in 25% of cases). Nearest neighbour on data source, outcome and public framing as a warning system.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Predictor is an AICc-selected abrupt shift in surplus production located with hindsight, not an AR1/variance score; no forecast origins, hold-out, hindcast, state/trend baseline, calibration or false-alarm budget; treatment of recent PAS with short follow-up (right-censoring) not visible; single realm. Its collapse thresholds join our sensitivity list.

closest_prior_work.citation: Zhang, F. (2020). Early warning signals of population productivity regime shifts in global fisheries. Ecological Indicators 115: 106371. doi:10.1016/j.ecolind.2020.106371. URL https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1470160X20303083 . Sole author per snippets; co-authors not visible. Confidence: medium (abstract-level only).
closest_prior_work.overlap: Same database (RAM Legacy, 191 populations) and same two indicators (SD, AR1); explicit TP/TN/lead-time questions and a positive likelihood ratio (implies a false-positive rate); >5 y warning for >50% of populations; SD and AR1 jointly detected in <50% of shifts.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Outcome is a productivity regime shift, not first abundance collapse; forecast origins, train/test split, non-EWS comparator, threshold calibration, operationalization of 'no shift' and series-end handling are all not visible in search results; single realm. Must be read in full before the novelty statement is frozen.

closest_prior_work.citation: Burthe, S. J., Henrys, P. A., Mackay, E. B., Spears, B. M., Campbell, R., Carvalho, L., Dudley, B., Gunn, I. D. M., Johns, D. G., Maberly, S. C., May, L., Newell, M. A., Wanless, S., Winfield, I. J., Thackeray, S. J. & Daunt, F. (2016). J. Appl. Ecol. 53(3): 666-676. doi:10.1111/1365-2664.12519. URL https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1365-2664.12519 . Confidence: high on numbers, medium on design inference.
closest_prior_work.overlap: 126 abundance series, 55 taxa, six UK aquatic systems; GAM-standardized series; turning points from GAM first derivative; variance and AR1 over a 25% rolling window; TP/FN/FP tallied within a 10-year window; TP uncommon (8%/6% of series; 9%/13% of cases); FP more prevalent than FN (53% vs 38% variance; 47% vs 40% AR); 43% of series classified differently by the two indicators.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Retrospective whole-series coherence analysis (GAM fitted to full series), no forecast origins, no hold-out, no baseline, no calibration, no false-alarm budget, outcome is any nonlinear turning point (not collapse, not directional), 10-year window rather than 1-5 y horizons, series-end handling not visible, six UK aquatic systems only.

closest_prior_work.citation: O'Brien, D. A., Deb, S., Gal, G., Thackeray, S. J., Dutta, P. S., Matsuzaki, S.-i. S., May, L. & Clements, C. F. (2023). Early warning signals have limited applicability to empirical lake data. Nature Communications 14: 7942. doi:10.1038/s41467-023-43744-8. URLs https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-023-43744-8 ; https://github.com/duncanobrien/ews-assessments . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Nine lake datasets (Kasumigaura, Kinneret, Loch Leven, Lower and Upper Zurich, Mendota, Monona, Washington, Windermere); rolling and expanding windows; univariate, multivariate and EWSNet indicators in transitioning and non-transitioning series; Bayesian binomial models against a 0.5 chance reference; unscaled EWSNet TP 0.93/0.89 but TN 0.19/0.05; ROC/precision-recall added in review; most indicators near chance; strong preprocessing dependence. Directly relevant to our lake challenge analysis.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Community regime shifts in lakes, not first population collapse; binary per-series fate rather than fixed-horizon sequential alarms; fixed alarm conventions (2-sigma expanding; Kendall tau) rather than thresholds calibrated to a common false-alarm burden; comparator is chance and other EWS families, not a state/trend forecast; no lead-time analysis; no censoring concept.

closest_prior_work.citation: Falmagne, Stephenson & Levin (2026). Interpretable early warnings using machine learning in an online game-experiment. PNAS 123(1): e2503493122 (published 6 Jan 2026); arXiv 2502.09880. doi:10.1073/pnas.2503493122. URL https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2503493122 . Author initials conflict between inputs (G./A.B. vs C./E.) and FPR 3.6% vs 3.7% - unresolved; confidence high on design, low on initials.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Design-wise the nearest template: gradient-boosted trees with memory-retaining features on multiple system-specific series; fixed detection window (half of transitions within 20 minutes); explicit false-positive rate (3.6%); trained on 2022 r/place, robust on the held-out 2023 event; reported to outperform standard EWS; SHAP recovers slowing down or speeding up.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Non-ecological online game at minute scale; no classical-EWS vs state/trend baseline at matched false-alarm burden; no population-abundance collapse, cross-realm data, system grouping or censoring logic.

closest_prior_work.citation: Deb, S., Sidheekh, S., Clements, C. F., Krishnan, N. C. & Dutta, P. S. (2022). Machine learning methods trained on simple models can predict critical transitions in complex natural systems. R. Soc. Open Sci. 9(2): 211475. doi:10.1098/rsos.211475. URLs https://doi.org/10.1098/rsos.211475 ; https://github.com/sahilsid/EWSNet . Confidence: medium.
closest_prior_work.overlap: EWSNet (LSTM+FCN) trained on nine dynamical models with catastrophic, non-catastrophic and no-transition classes; compared with logistic regression, SVM, random forest and MLP trained on EWS trend statistics; applied to real series 'from rapid climatic change to the collapse of ecological populations' (6 of 8 climate series correct).
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Every comparator is fed EWS-derived features, so no state/trend baseline; no sequential origins or calendar horizon; ecological test datasets and per-dataset false-alarm rates not visible; O'Brien 2023 reports EWSNet TN 0.05-0.2 on lakes.

closest_prior_work.citation: Pinsky, M. L. & Byler, D. (2015). Fishing, fast growth and climate variability increase the risk of collapse. Proc. R. Soc. B 282(1813): 20151053. URL https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rspb/article/282/1813/20151053/84303/Fishing-fast-growth-and-climate-variability ; data https://datadryad.org/dataset/doi:10.5061/dryad.d5f53 . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Boosted regression trees predicting collapse vs depletion across 154 RAM Legacy v1.0 populations (1950-2008) from fishing pressure, growth rate and climate variability, non-collapsing populations included; the natural 'state-and-pressure' comparator for the fisheries arm.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: No EWS predictors; forecast origins, hold-out, horizon, calibration, false-alarm budget and exact collapse thresholds not visible (an unattributed snippet mentioning BMIN < 20% BMSY / B/BMSY < 0.5 must not be attributed to it without checking).

closest_prior_work.citation: Ward, E. J., Holmes, E. E., Thorson, J. T. & Collen, B. (2014). Complexity is costly. Oikos 123(6): 652-661. doi:10.1111/j.1600-0706.2014.00916.x. Full text read: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eeholmes/eeholmes.github.io/master/publications/Wardetal2014.pdf ; code https://github.com/eric-ward/complexity-costly ; reproduction http://opetchey.github.io/RREEBES/WARD_etal_2014_Oikos/report/Ward_2014_report.html . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: 2379 vertebrate index series (LPI, BBS, RSPB, RAM Legacy recruits-per-spawner, Pacific salmon); 49 models; fit to all but the last five observations; 1-5-step forecasts scored by MASE against a random walk without drift; the last observation was the most accurate forecast except for cyclic salmon; ARIMA/GAM similar to RW and worsening at 2-4 steps. Strongest precedent for our state baseline and capacity-matching concern.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: No event outcome, no EWS predictors (AR1 and variance appear only as covariates of forecast error), no alarms or false-alarm budget, no calibration, one origin per series.

closest_prior_work.citation: Bury, T. M., Sujith, R. I., Pavithran, I., Scheffer, M., Lenton, T. M., Anand, M. & Bauch, C. T. (2021). Deep learning for early warning signals of tipping points. PNAS 118(39): e2106140118. Code https://github.com/ThomasMBury/deep-early-warnings-pnas (published text not seen). Confidence: medium.
closest_prior_work.overlap: CNN-LSTM trained on 500,000/200,000 synthetic series with a null class; applied incrementally along series; ROC/AUC against Kendall-tau of rolling variance and AR1; null simulations, AR(1) surrogates and quasi-static experiments as negatives.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: No population monitoring data (May/consumer-resource/SEIRx models; thermoacoustic, paleoclimate, sediment records); windows placed as fractions of the known pre-transition record; detrending uses the whole pre-transition series; no state/trend baseline; threshold-free AUC, no false-alarm budget; Dablander & Bury 2022 show detrending-filter learning.

closest_prior_work.citation: Litzow, M. A., Mueter, F. J. & Urban, J. D. (2013). Rising catch variability preceded historical fisheries collapses in Alaska. Ecological Applications 23: 1475-1487. doi:10.1890/12-0670.1. URL https://doi.org/10.1890/12-0670.1 . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: 14 Gulf of Alaska/Bering Sea crustacean fisheries (12 collapsing, 2 non-collapsing); rising spatial catch variability 1-4 y before collapse in a random-effects model; individual trends significant in only 4 of 12; variability trends differed between collapsing and non-collapsing fisheries.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Retrospective alignment on known collapse dates; spatial not temporal variance; only two negatives; no origins, hold-out, baseline or calibration.

closest_prior_work.citation: Hefley, T. J., Tyre, A. J. & Blankenship, E. E. (2013). Statistical indicators and state-space population models predict extinction in a population of bobwhite quail. Theoretical Ecology 6: 319-331. doi:10.1007/s12080-013-0195-3. URL https://doi.org/10.1007/s12080-013-0195-3 . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: The one wild-population study pairing an EWS-type indicator with a state-space threshold-crossing estimate (threshold crossed 2010, 95% CI 2002-2036; 2008 in a second dataset).
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: n = 1 population, no negatives, no comparative skill test of indicator vs state-space model, no origins, horizon, calibration or false-alarm accounting.

Ecology Letters 10: 1182-1198. doi:10.1111/j.1461-0248.2007.01105.x; with Holmes et al. (2005) NOAA Tech. Memo. NMFS-NWFSC-67 https://repository.library.noaa.gov/view/noaa/3422/noaa_3422_DS1.pdf . Confidence: high (2007), medium (2005).
closest_prior_work.overlap: 63 empirical series (>=30 y) split into a 20-year parameterization period and 10/20/30-year forecast periods; diffusion-approximation quasi-extinction risk relatively unbiased with usefully narrow intervals; closest precedent for an out-of-sample threshold-crossing forecast on real population series.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Single split per series, no EWS comparator, no alarms or false-alarm budget; data source not visible.

closest_prior_work.citation: Buelo, C. D. et al. (2022). Ecological Applications 32(5): e2616, doi:10.1002/eap.2616; Pace, M. L. et al. (2017). PNAS 114, doi:10.1073/pnas.1612424114; Wilkinson, G. M. et al. (2018). Ecological Monographs 88: 188-203, doi:10.1002/ecm.1286. URLs https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/eap.2616 ; https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.1612424114 ; https://doi.org/10.1002/ecm.1286 . Confidence: high.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Whole-lake experiments with reference lakes: true-positive alarm rates 2.5-8.3x false-positive rates for rolling SD but not for rolling AR (Buelo); the one field study with a preset prospective alarm threshold applied in real time (Pace, n = 1 lake); sequential quickest-detection alarms with 1-57-day lead across six enrichments (Wilkinson).
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Ecosystem-level blooms in a handful of manipulated lakes; no population collapse; thresholds preset or reference-based, not calibrated across many systems; no state/trend baseline.

closest_prior_work.citation: Jarvis-Cross, M., Kirk, D., Krichel, L., Luijckx, P., Molnár, P. K. & Krkošek, M. (2025). Early warning signals do not predict a warming-induced experimental epidemic. PLOS Global Public Health 5(10): e0005142 (8 Oct 2025; bioRxiv 2025.04.14.648789). doi:10.1371/journal.pgph.0005142. Confidence: high (sweeps 0, 9, 11, 12 and refutation A agree; Angle D's 'authors not visible / preprint' entry is superseded).
closest_prior_work.overlap: Daphnia magna-Ordospora colligata experiment with 4 control and 4 warming populations plus 1,000 simulated each; EWS of epidemic emergence detected nearly as often in sub-epidemic-temperature controls as in warming populations; explicit false-positive framing.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Epidemic emergence in a laboratory system, not abundance collapse in wild monitored populations; no sequential fixed-horizon prediction, baseline or matched false-alarm calibration.

closest_prior_work.citation: Ma, Z., Zeng, C., Zhang, Y.-C. & Bury, T. M. (2025). Predicting critical transitions with machine learning trained on surrogates of historical data. Communications Physics 8: 258 (arXiv 2410.09707). URL https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-025-02172-4 ; code https://github.com/ZhiqinMa/surrogate_data_based_machine_learning . Confidence: high on attribution (sweeps agree with Angle D's correction), medium on content.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Classifiers trained on surrogates of past transitions report higher sensitivity and specificity than variance and lag-1 AC, i.e., specificity-aware comparison against exactly our two classical indicators.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Empirical data from geology, climatology, sociology and cardiology (chick heart, sediment archive, paleoclimate, tree rings); no ecological population data; comparator is classical EWS, not a state/trend forecast; no fixed-horizon sequential design or common false-alarm budget.

closest_prior_work.citation: Mullett, D. (2026). Benchmarking Recursive-Collapse Warning Claims Under Matched False-Positive Control (Loopzero). arXiv 2606.00329 v2. closest_prior_work.overlap: Methodological neighbour: detectors evaluated under a locked, pre-registered equal-false-positive contract (FP in [0.03, 0.07]) on frozen public benchmarks, the same 'same false-alarm burden' logic as our calibration.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Market telemetry and a recommender replay; no ecology, population collapse or EWS vs state/trend baseline. Cite only as precedent for matched-false-positive benchmarking.

closest_prior_work.citation: TipPFN: In-context learning to predict critical transitions in dynamical systems. arXiv 2605.12308 (12 May 2026). URL https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12308 . Author attribution conflicts between inputs (audit/sweep 8: 'Sevinchan, Y. and 10 others'; Angle D: 'Ramien, G. et al.'); unresolved, confidence low on authorship, medium on content.
closest_prior_work.overlap: Prior-data-fitted transformer trained on a synthetic bifurcation generator; reported to beat classical EWS and existing deep classifiers across 14 semi-real, sim-to-real and real systems (climate, engineering, biology); Angle D snippet reports 406 systems/2,776 episodes with 226 real positive and 799 real negative samples, so real non-transitioning series are scored.
closest_prior_work.gap_we_fill: Whether any monitored population series (RAM/GPDD/LPD/BioTIME) are among the real systems is not visible; no prequential origins with calendar horizons, no state/trend comparator, no calibration to a common false-alarm budget.

design_lessons: Include a last-value (random walk without drift) risk score in the baseline set and report MASE-like skill alongside alarm metrics: on 2379 vertebrate series the last observation was the most accurate 1-5-step forecast and added parameters cost accuracy (Ward et al. 2014, full text https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eeholmes/eeholmes.github.io/master/publications/Wardetal2014.pdf; high).

Count false alarms as false alarms with a frozen budget and complete follow-up: Cano et al. 2025 relabel predicted-abrupt non-abrupt series as 'at risk' with no follow-up (https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2505461122; high) and Pélissié et al. 2026 report that 31 of 42 negative productivity shifts were not followed by collapse (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13537261/; high); these numbers motivate the operating-point analysis.

Bracket the conventional forecast between an idealized upper bound and a phenomenological lower bound, after Lapeyrolerie & Boettiger 2023 (true-model MCMC vs ARIMA; RNN/Transformer forecasts resembled naive last-state extrapolation and were accurate 'right up to the transition'; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/boettiger-lab/mee_tipping_point_forecasting/main/manuscript/manuscript.Rmd; high).

Preregister a collapse-definition family, adding Pélissié's 25%-of-to-date-average (with 10% of max, 15% and 50% of average) and Pinsky 2011's Bmin < 0.2 BMSY to the sensitivity list (URLs in collapse_definitions_in_literature; high).

Treat association windows as the retrospective analogue of the horizon: Burthe's 10-year window (medium) and Pélissié's 4-12-year observed lead distribution (medium, version-dependent) bracket the 1-5-year primary horizon and support a 6-10-year secondary horizon.

Keep the critical-speeding-up score separate and directional: the Entropy 2026 review notes fold-bifurcation/depensatory fish dynamics can invert classical EWS (https://doi.org/10.3390/e28060628; medium); Titus & Watson 2020 and Wagner & Eisenman 2015 give the theoretical basis (audit Section 9; medium).

State that RAM-derived origins are 'as finally assessed': a 2024 Science paper (authors not visible) reports assessment models overstate sustainability and 85% more stocks than recognized have likely collapsed below 10% of maximum historical biomass, so the series available at time t differs from the final series; survey-index robustness analyses therefore matter (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adl6282; medium).

Freeze preprocessing before any classifier is applied and reproduce each classifier's documented preprocessing exactly: Dablander & Bury 2022 showed the Bury 2021 classifier learned detrending-filter features (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2207720119; medium).

Enforce the complete-window rule and a mean-removal transform: a 2025 arXiv/2026 Science Advances analysis (authors not visible) shows agreement between variance- and AR1-based indicators is driven by the series' initial data point and weakened by missing values and outliers (https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19034; medium).

Include rate-induced transitions and stochastic (noise-driven) transitions in the Section 12 falsification suite, where critical slowing down is not expected (Huang et al. 2024, https://www.nature.com/articles/s42256-024-00937-0; Boettiger & Hastings 2013 'no early warning for stochastic transitions', https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2013.1372; high on existence).

Answer the prosecutor's fallacy explicitly: selecting systems because they transitioned inflates false-positive rates of warning statistics (Boettiger & Hastings 2012, https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2012.2085; high); the risk-set design with all monitored systems is the remedy and should be named as such.

Borrow named evaluation conventions rather than reinvent them: landmarking / discrete-time person-period labels (van Houwelingen 2007; Suresh et al. 2022), IPCW time-dependent AUC and Brier for any censored sensitivity (Blanche et al. 2015), sensitivity at a fixed false-prediction rate with event-time surrogates as the chance null (Winterhalder 2003; Andrzejak 2003; Schelter 2006), paired AUC tests for clustered data (Obuchowski 1997), Riley et al. 2021 sample-size targets and Van Calster calibration hierarchy (audit Section 10; medium, snippet-level).

Use a matched-false-positive contract as a documented precedent from outside ecology (Mullett 2026, FP in [0.03, 0.07], https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.00329; medium) and horizon-specific ROC skill (Ashwin et al. 2025, https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rspa.2025.0405; medium), citing both as methodological neighbours only.

Prefer rolling over expanding windows for imminent transitions but keep expanding windows as a robustness variant: the Entropy 2026 review reports rolling windows generally outperform expanding windows, while O'Brien et al. 2023 note expanding windows mitigate false positives from short series (medium).

Expect a fraction of first collapses to be unforecastable shocks and bound achievable sensitivity accordingly: black-swan events are mainly crashes (Anderson et al. 2017) and severe die-offs occur at roughly 14% per generation (Reed et al. 2003) (audit Section 11; medium).

Capture state-and-trend signals of approaching extinction in B1 so EWS are not credited for them: rate of decline and growth-rate variability increase as extinction approaches (Fagan & Holmes 2006, https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1461-0248.2005.00845.x; high).

Consider Masuda 2026 TIPMOC (sequential variance-only test with explicit false-positive control; https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/4/pgag126/8654731; high on existence) as a secondary sequential EWS, noting the authors did not apply it to empirical data.
Use Capdevila/O'Brien et al. 2026 per-population threat annotations (code https://github.com/duncanobrien/multiple-threats) as outcome-blind annotations for the mechanism analysis (medium).
baseline_conventions_found: Random walk without drift (last observed value) as the explicit benchmark, scored by MASE at 1-5 steps; plus random walk with drift, state-space random walks (StructTS, MARSS), ARIMA(p,d,q), GAM, exponential smoothing, neural nets, random forest, Simplex/S-map among 49 models (Ward et al. 2014; full text; high).

Diffusion-approximation quasi-extinction (threshold-crossing) forecasts parameterized on 20 years and validated over 10/20/30-year windows, single split per series (Holmes et al. 2007; Holmes et al. 2005 NOAA cross-validation; high/medium).
State-space population model estimating the year of extinction-threshold crossing, corroborated by a statistical indicator, in one wild quail population (Hefley et al. 2013; high).

Boosted regression trees on fishing pressure (chronic vs acute overfishing), growth rate and climate variability predicting collapse vs depletion across 154 RAM Legacy populations (Pinsky & Byler 2015; high); Burgess et al. 2013 T-score from life history and effort (medium).

Probability of stock increase as a function of stock size and fishing pressure (Hilborn et al. 2014; high) and a null model of natural fluctuations for collapse frequency (Essington et al. 2015; high).
Naive-forecast MASE in hindcasting cross-validation with sequential tail-cutting of recent years (HCXval; PLOS ONE 2024, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0302576, authors not visible; low).

Random-walk and day-of-year climatology nulls with CRPS at each horizon in the NEON Ecological Forecasting Challenge (Thomas et al. 2023; Olsson et al. 2025; medium) and naive baselines in BBS/Portal hindcasts (Harris et al. 2018; White et al. 2019; medium).
ARIMA as lower bound and true-model MCMC as upper bound for probabilistic forecasts through transitions (Lapeyrolerie & Boettiger 2023; high).

Kendall-tau trends of rolling variance and lag-1 autocorrelation as the comparator for learned classifiers, with fixed-parameter null simulations, AR(1) surrogates or quasi-static segments as negatives (Bury et al. 2021; medium); surrogate-trained classifiers vs variance/AC with sensitivity and specificity (Ma et al. 2025; medium).
A 0.5 chance reference in Bayesian binomial success models, with true-positive and true-negative probabilities reported separately (O'Brien et al. 2023; high).

Unmanipulated reference lakes as negative controls and sequential quickest-detection alarms against the reference (Carpenter et al. 2011; Seekell et al. 2012; Wilkinson et al. 2018; Buelo et al. 2022; high).
Experimental control populations as non-transitioning negatives (Drake & Griffen 2010; Jarvis-Cross et al. 2025; high).
Classical ML classifiers (logistic regression, SVM, random forest, MLP) trained on EWS trend features as comparators for EWSNet (Deb et al. 2022; medium).
Leave-timepoint-out and leave-one-out out-of-sample predictions in hierarchical GP-EDM (GPEDM package; high) and EDM vs conventional stock-recruitment models (Munch et al. 2018; medium).
collapse_definitions_in_literature: Biomass in a given year below 25% of the average stock biomass recorded to date; robustness at 10% of maximum biomass and 15% and 50% of average biomass (Pélissié et al. 2026; https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed7911; single snippet, medium).
Biomass falling to one quarter or less of the stock's average biomass, 27 of 55 forage fish stocks (Essington et al. 2015; https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1422020112; high).

Minimum annual biomass below 20% of BMSY, 223 assessments (Pinsky et al. 2011; https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1015313108; high). An unattributed snippet mentioning 'BMIN < 20% BMSY' and 'B/BMSY < 0.5' must not be attributed to Pinsky & Byler 2015 without checking (sweep 2 notes).
Depletion below 20% of maximum observed stock size (Hilborn et al. 2014; https://academic.oup.com/icesjms/article/71/8/2141/754978; high).

Biomass below 10% of maximum historical biomass, with 85% more stocks than recognized likely collapsed once retrospective bias is accounted for (Science 2024, authors not visible; https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adl6282; medium).

Reported catch at or below 10% of the historical maximum (Worm et al. 2006; https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=961611; high), criticized as an artefact by Branch et al. 2011 (medium); catch-series typology across 1519 FAO series (Mullon et al. 2005; details not visible).

Stocks falling below 50% (119 of 373) and 15% (29) of their historical average biomass in RAM Legacy v4.44 (Rocha et al. manuscript, https://github.com/juanrocha/marine_tipping; high on the repository text; unpublished).
80-90% declines described as commonly used operational thresholds for population collapse (snippet associated with Cerini et al. 2023/2025; medium).
Significant nonlinear turning points from the first derivative of a GAM smooth, any direction (Burthe et al. 2016; high on method, direction not visible).
Critical transition = TGAM breakpoint in plankton density matched by a state-space breakpoint plus bimodality and hysteresis; 'abrupt non-bifurcation' otherwise (O'Brien et al. 2023; high).

Abrupt trajectory class by AICc among no-change/linear/quadratic/abrupt with asdetect confirmation within 5 years, productivity or CPUE (Cano et al. 2025; Pélissié, Devictor & Dakos 2024 framework; high).
Productivity regime shifts in RAM Legacy populations, detection method not visible (Zhang 2020; medium); STARS-type productivity regime shifts (Vert-pre et al. 2013; high).

Quasi-extinction: decline to a critical threshold within the forecast period (Holmes et al. 2007; high); witnessed extinction after >=12 years of monitoring (Fagan & Holmes 2006; high); trajectory-shape diagnosis of rapid declines (Di Fonzo et al. 2013; medium).

This study's proposal (not frozen): 0.20 x trailing reference with 2-year persistence, i.e., an 80% decline from a trailing-median reference (STAGE0_REPORT Section 6; reports/stage0_proposed_parameters.md), which sits inside the family above.

unresolved_uncertainties: No full text was read for any paper except Ward et al. 2014 and Lapeyrolerie & Boettiger 2023; all design judgments about Zhang 2020, Cano 2025, Pélissié 2026, Burthe 2016, O'Brien 2023, Bury 2021, Deb 2022 and Falmagne 2026 rest on snippets, abstracts and public code and must be confirmed against published methods and supplements (PNAS SI, Science Advances SM, Zenodo R script) by a reader with publisher access.

Zhang 2020 methods (forecast origins, 'no regime shift' operationalization, alarm threshold, series-end handling, co-authors, data/code availability) are entirely not visible; threat rating stays moderate until read.

Whether the published Cano et al. 2025 analysis used the code default cut=TRUE with 'asclassif' detrending (label-informed truncation of abrupt-class series) is not visible; if so the LOO AUCs partly reflect label leakage, which matters for how we cite them.

Pélissié et al. 2026 handling of right-censored stocks (recent negative PAS with short follow-up), the statistical test behind the 23% vs 12% comparison, whether 'first' collapse only was used, and the Zenodo record content are not visible.
